prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as the sole prize part and the same three names. After round 1 my reasons are sharper, not different. The discovery is a quantitative prediction, the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011, followed by nature giving the answer in 2018: correlated insulators and superconductivity at the predicted twist angle, in a device where the angle is a control knob. That is a clue from nature, not thinking alone, and it is the discovery-first story I look for. The phenomenology has been reproduced by many independent groups, across graphene multilayers and other moire systems, and the committee majority has converged on the same trio without being pushed to. The chair asks for a common standard for maturity. Mine is this: the claim being honoured must be one that independent laboratories agree on, and the citation must claim nothing beyond it. The citation I propose claims the prediction and the existence and tunability of the correlated and superconducting phases, not the pairing mechanism and not the whole moire field. Held to that standard, B033 passes. The Nobel Prize has honoured observed phenomena before their mechanism was understood, and I am not persuaded that this case needs a different rule.
statement.case_against: I have not resolved the attribution at the third seat and I will not pretend to. Andrei's pre-2018 STM and transport work on twisted layers is a real experimental strand, and the three-person limit leaves out Andrei, the first authors of the 2018 papers, and the Dean and Kim hBN device work. Sample dependence is also a real limit: twist-angle disorder and strain mean the phase diagram varies from device to device, which Kroll and Lindroth rightly press, and the pairing mechanism is open. If the committee finds that Andrei's work showed the correlated phases at or near the magic angle before 2018, the configuration fails on credit and not on science, and I would want to revisit the third name. On the record as the members describe it, her work showed flat-band-like features and Van Hove singularities but not the correlated or superconducting states, so I judge the claim real but not decisive for this citation. The risk is that this judgement rests on my memory and on colleagues in condensed matter, and a hindsight view could be harsher.

responses.point: Lindroth asks what distinguishes the maturity of B033 from that of B026, and says intercomparison of clocks at 1e-18 is the verification the committee asks for, while moire results depend on device-to-device twist-angle disorder.
responses.response: This is a fair question and I will answer it directly. The two cases pass the same test in different ways. For clocks, independent laboratories agree numerically at 1e-18 on a measured number. For moire graphene, many independent laboratories find the same qualitative phase diagram, correlated insulators next to superconducting domes near the magic angle, even though the quantitative details such as the exact angle and the carrier density at which the dome appears vary with the sample. What I require is that the claim in the citation be the part that is reproduced. So the citation names the prediction and the existence of the phases, and not the precise phase boundaries or the mechanism. I accept that clocks are the cleaner verification. I do not accept that this makes B033 premature, because the thing we would honour is not the thing that varies. My earlier hesitation about B026 stands on a different axis: whether it is a new discovery or a continuation of 2005 and 2012. Your argument that the magic wavelength solves a different problem from the comb or the single ion is persuasive, and I now regard B026 as the strongest fallback and no longer merely a serious one.

responses.point: Kroll says twist-angle disorder and strain make sample-to-sample variation in the moire phase diagram large, so the experimental credit is harder to pin down than for a clock, and he keeps B033 as first alternative.
responses.response: I agree with the facts and I think the right answer is in the citation wording and not in delay. Sample variation makes it harder to say which feature is intrinsic, and that is why I would not let the citation speak about mechanism or about quantitative phase boundaries. I would also note that the experiments that settled the discovery were not single devices: later work on cleaner, better-controlled samples and on other multilayer systems found the same insulators and superconductivity, which is the independent confirmation you ask for in a clock. Where I do give ground is the experimental credit: for a clock, the instrument is the discovery and two names map onto it, whereas here three names cannot cover every experimental contributor. That is a limit of the three-person rule and not a weakness in the science. If the committee agrees with you and decides that this attribution cannot be defended, your fallback of B026 is mine too.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from Andrei to Bistritzer in round 1, but says the choice is arguable, defers to colleagues, and flags that continuum-model flat bands may be quantitatively affected by lattice relaxation and strain.
responses.response: I agree with the move to Bistritzer and the reason given: a prediction made by two authors in one paper cannot sensibly be split. On your relaxation point, I think it supports the citation rather than undermining it. The continuum model got the existence of the magic-angle flat bands right, and later relaxation and strain work refined the details, which is the normal life of a good prediction. The citation should say flat bands at a magic angle and stop there. Since the chair asks whether anyone can say what Andrei's work showed, I will say what I believe and flag the limit: her group saw localisation signatures and Van Hove singularities in twisted layers by STM before 2018, which established that the twist matters, but not the correlated insulating state or superconductivity. As the specialist you should confirm or correct that, and if you judge her results closer to the prediction than I do, I would want to hear it before the vote.

responses.point: Olsson says the rule is to find the original experiment even if it was not the most elegant, so the committee should establish what Andrei's group showed and when, and she accepts the trio if the record shows a precursor and not the discovery of the correlated phases.
responses.response: I accept your rule and I think it is the right test: who first observed the phenomenon the citation names. Here the phenomenon is correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, and on the evidence we have the first observation is the 2018 work. Andrei's earlier work is a precursor on flat-band physics and I would say so in the committee's own record, so that the choice is documented and not silent. I would add one point of difference. The discovery is not only an experiment. A prize that keeps MacDonald and Bistritzer together with Jarillo-Herrero keeps the theory and the decisive measurement in one citation, and that is how I would defend the choice if challenged from outside. I also agree with you and Mehlig that we should not write wording that suggests the field began in 2018.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether anyone wants to revive B024 or B010, and notes that he moved off B024 on attribution grounds.
responses.response: I do not wish to revive either. On IceCube I still find a one-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds hard to defend, and the source identification is not yet at the level I would want, so I would let the field mature and see what a second detector confirms. On circuit QED the 2025 prize is too close, as Johansson himself accepted. I would add that your move off your own opening first choice is the right kind of change: you moved because of an argument about credit, and not because of a vote count. I will do the same only if someone shows that Andrei's early work belongs in the citation.

uncertainties: Whether Andrei's pre-2018 STM and transport results are close enough to the correlated phases to deserve a laureate seat; my judgement that they are not rests on memory and on colleagues' accounts and has not been verified.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism and device-to-device variation will make recognition now look premature in hindsight.
Whether the committee can defend leaving out the first authors of the 2018 papers and the Dean and Kim hBN device work under the three-person limit.
Whether B026 will be read outside the committee as a new discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the pending redefinition of the second should count for or against it.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no collaboration or institutional tie to any credited candidate on the shortlist. My research is in string theory and cosmology. I trained with David Gross, who is not on the shortlist. As Secretary I should be careful that my procedural role does not weigh in favour of any candidate, and I do not treat the first-place count as a substitute for the scientific and attribution judgements above.
